 Artemis II Ionosphere Hit: 3.7 TECU, No GPS Outage [2026]
 Priya Anand 
 Updated Nov 4, 2026 · 17 min read 
 Headlines this week say NASA’s Artemis II moon rocket “tore a hole” in Earth’s upper atmosphere and knocked out GPS. The research record behind the story says something narrower and, for engineers, more interesting. Scientists detected ionospheric disturbances tied to three Artemis II events: the April 1, 2026 launch from Kennedy Space Center, the Apogee Raise Maneuver (ARM), and the Trans-Lunar Injection (TLI) burn. They found those disturbances by reading GPS and GLONASS signals, which means the satellites were the measuring tape, not the casualty.

 That distinction matters for anyone who builds on satellite timing or navigation. Space and Chosun Ilbo both carried the dramatic version of the story, and it spread fast. Yet the verified material shows no documented GPS outage, no degraded service report, and no on-record statement from a NASA official saying Artemis II disrupted navigation. We covered the mission’s hardware side earlier, including the 252,756-mile record and the heat shield result . This piece covers the atmospheric footprint and sorts what is measured from what is merely repeated.
 Below you will find the confirmed numbers, the unconfirmed claims, the physics that links a rocket plume to a shift in electron content, and what it all means for hardware makers, satellite operators and anyone filing a story about it. Our hardware coverage follows the same rule throughout: if a figure is not in a source we can name, we say so.

 Add now What the Artemis II Ionosphere Research Actually Found
 The core finding is a set of measured ionospheric disturbances linked to the Artemis II flight. Researchers reported effects at three points in the mission timeline. The first came at launch on April 1, 2026, when NASA’s Space Launch System (SLS) rocket lifted Orion off from Kennedy Space Center. The second followed the Apogee Raise Maneuver, an engine burn that lifted the spacecraft’s high point in its early orbit. The third followed Trans-Lunar Injection, the burn that sent Orion toward the Moon.
 Each event left a mark in total electron content (TEC), the count of free electrons along a path through the ionosphere. The team built its TEC maps from GPS and GLONASS observations. For the ARM and TLI events, the reported disturbance amplitudes ran from roughly 2.5 to 3.7 TECU. For the ARM event, the disturbance stretched across about 50 degrees of longitude over North America. For the launch itself, the researchers described acoustic and gravity-wave effects that moved at 600 to 1,500 meters per second and lasted 15 to 20 minutes.

 Those numbers describe a real, measurable perturbation. They do not describe a rupture. The word “hole” appears in the viral headline, and the verified record does not use it for Artemis II. Treat it as a headline flourish until a named researcher or agency says otherwise on the record.
 Three Events, Three Signatures: Launch, ARM and TLI
 The three disturbances are not the same animal. A launch drives pressure waves up from the ground and through the lower atmosphere, and those waves reach ionospheric heights after minutes. An in-space burn like ARM or TLI works differently, because the engine exhaust is released directly at altitude and perturbs the plasma where it already sits. Researchers who study these effects treat them as separate mechanisms, so it helps to tabulate what the record says for each one.
 Artemis II event Reported effect Reported scale Detection data 
 Launch (April 1, 2026, Kennedy Space Center) Acoustic and gravity-wave disturbances Speeds of 600 to 1,500 m/s, lasting 15 to 20 minutes GPS and GLONASS TEC 
 Apogee Raise Maneuver (ARM) Ionospheric disturbance over North America About 50 degrees of longitude, roughly 2.5 to 3.7 TECU GPS and GLONASS TEC 
 Trans-Lunar Injection (TLI) Ionospheric disturbance Roughly 2.5 to 3.7 TECU GPS and GLONASS TEC 
 GPS service impact No documented outage or degradation Not applicable Not confirmed in available record 
 “Hole” in the upper atmosphere Headline wording only No measurement uses this term Not confirmed in available record 
 The last two rows carry the weight of this article. Everything above them is a measurement. Everything in those rows is a claim that sits outside the confirmed record.
 Why GPS and GLONASS Can Detect Ionospheric Disturbances
 Navigation satellites broadcast on more than one frequency. Radio signals slow down slightly as they cross the ionosphere, and the delay depends on frequency. By comparing the delay on two frequencies, a ground receiver can compute how many electrons sat along the path between it and the satellite. That number is slant TEC. Scientists have used the trick for years to watch storms, earthquakes and rocket launches without flying a single dedicated instrument.
 How a receiver turns delay into TEC
 One TECU equals 10^16 electrons per square meter along the signal path. A network of receivers on the ground sees many satellite paths at once, so researchers can stitch the individual slices into a map and watch a disturbance travel. Using GLONASS alongside GPS adds more satellites and more crossing paths, which sharpens the picture. That is why the Artemis II study leaned on both constellations.
 What 2.5 to 3.7 TECU looks like in context
 An amplitude of 2.5 to 3.7 TECU is a modest bump on the scale ionospheric scientists work with. The unit’s size gives a sense of it, because a few TECU is the kind of variation that precision positioning systems already model and correct for. I am not claiming a threshold here, since the verified material gives none. The point is simply that the amplitude reads as a detectable perturbation, and the research record reports it as one, not as a failure mode for navigation.
 The same logic explains the headline problem. A receiver that can measure a disturbance has, by definition, kept working well enough to take the measurement. Detection through GPS is evidence that GPS functioned, not evidence that it broke.
 The “Hole in the Atmosphere” Claim: What the Record Supports
 Let’s go through the viral claims one at a time and compare them with the fact sheet. The story as it traveled said that the Artemis II launch tore a hole in Earth’s upper atmosphere, that the hole was huge, and that it disrupted GPS. The verified record supports a piece of the first idea in a loose sense, since rockets can locally deplete or disturb ionospheric electron content. It does not support the size claim or the GPS claim.
 Claim in circulation Status What the record shows 
 Artemis II launched April 1, 2026 from Kennedy Space Center on SLS and Orion Confirmed Mission facts match the research summary 
 Disturbances tied to launch, ARM and TLI Confirmed Reported by researchers using GPS and GLONASS TEC 
 ARM disturbance spanned about 50 degrees of longitude over North America Confirmed Reported extent 
 ARM and TLI amplitudes of roughly 2.5 to 3.7 TECU Confirmed Reported amplitudes 
 Launch waves traveled at 600 to 1,500 m/s for 15 to 20 minutes Confirmed Reported wave behavior 
 Launch “tore a hole” in the upper atmosphere Unconfirmed Headline wording, not a measured result 
 Disturbance was “so huge” it disrupted GPS Unconfirmed No documented GPS outage or degradation 
 3,500 GPS stations affected over 5,000 km Unconfirmed Appears in a secondary report only 
 On-record NASA or researcher quote on GPS disruption Unconfirmed None located in the available material 
 The pattern is easy to spot. Every row marked confirmed describes something researchers measured. Every row marked unconfirmed describes something a headline asserted. When you read a space story, that split is the fastest quality check you have.
 Did Artemis II Disrupt GPS? The Evidence Gap
 The short answer is that nobody has shown it. The available record supports GPS-based detection of ionospheric variations. It does not document a GPS outage, a loss of fix, a timing error report or a service advisory tied to the launch. The verified material contains no named official confirming a disruption, whatever the coverage in Space or Chosun Ilbo implied.
 Engineers should find that unsurprising. Modern receivers already work through ionospheric variation every day. Dual-frequency units cancel most of the delay directly. Single-frequency phones lean on broadcast correction models that capture the average behavior. A short-lived, regional bump of a few TECU would, on its face, sit inside what those systems tolerate. I cannot prove that for Artemis II because the verified sources do not include receiver performance data. What I can say is that the claim of disruption has no evidence behind it yet, and the claim of detection has plenty.
 If you run a navigation-dependent service, the practical move is to check your own logs for April 1, 2026 and the burn windows rather than trust a headline. Precision agriculture, surveying and aviation users keep position-quality records. Those records would show a real effect long before a news cycle would.
 The 3,500 Stations and 5,000 km Figures
 Two numbers have been bouncing around social posts: 3,500 GPS stations and a 5,000 km reach. They appear in a secondary report. The authoritative material available for this article does not corroborate either one, so I am not repeating them as fact. The checked ARM figure is the 50 degrees of longitude across North America, and that is a longitude span, not a distance in kilometers.
 It is tempting to convert degrees to kilometers and declare the numbers consistent. I would not. The conversion depends on latitude, and the researchers have not published a distance claim in the verified record. A station count is also a different kind of number. It describes network coverage, meaning how many receivers happened to be in range, not how strong the disturbance was. A large station count would say the network was dense, not that anything went wrong.
 Until a primary source states these figures, treat them as unverified. Publishing them without that anchor is how a decent measurement paper turns into a viral outage story.
 SLS Thrust and the Physics Behind Launch-Driven Waves
 The SLS core stage is listed with 8,896 kN of thrust. That figure covers the core stage alone and does not include the side boosters, so it should not be read as the total liftoff force. It does give a sense of why researchers pay attention. A vehicle that pushes that much exhaust through the atmosphere launches a pressure wave that rises, thins and grows in amplitude as the air gets less dense.
 Those waves reach ionospheric heights and shove charged particles around. That produces the acoustic and gravity-wave signatures the Artemis II team reported, moving at 600 to 1,500 m/s and fading within 15 to 20 minutes. The speed range is broad because different wave types travel at different speeds, and the air they cross changes with altitude.

 In-space burns like ARM and TLI add a second route. Exhaust released at altitude injects gas directly into the ionosphere, and certain exhaust species can react with ionospheric ions and remove electrons. That is a general physics point, and the verified record does not tell us which mechanism dominated for Artemis II. It does tell us the effect lasted long enough and spread widely enough, about 50 degrees of longitude for ARM, for a ground network to map it.
 Historical Context: Rockets and the Ionosphere
 Artemis II did not invent this phenomenon. Scientists have studied rocket-induced ionospheric holes since the 1970s, after large launches were found to carve out electron-poor regions that persisted for a while. The field grew as GPS receiver networks spread, because dense ground arrays made it possible to watch launches in near real time. Researchers now treat every heavy-lift flight as a free experiment.
 What has changed is the audience. A decade ago, a paper about TEC perturbations circulated among a few hundred specialists. Today a launch pulls in a global audience, so a paper with a careful abstract reaches the public as a two-line headline within a day. The Artemis II case shows how that compression works. A careful statement, “ionospheric disturbances detected with GPS and GLONASS TEC,” gets rewritten into “launch tears hole in atmosphere, disrupts GPS.” Each rewrite sounds plausible, and each drops a layer of precision.
 Other spaceflight stories in recent weeks show the same atmospheric thread from a different angle. Our report on Swift’s failed rescue and three re-entry forecasts covers a spacecraft coming down through that same upper atmosphere, a reminder that the region above 100 km is busy with traffic going both ways.
 Market Impact: Who Cares About Ionospheric Data
 Ionospheric science sounds academic, but several industries pay attention to it. Precision positioning vendors correct for ionospheric delay in their products. Satellite operators track electron density because it affects radio links. Defense planners care about anything that touches navigation in contested regions. And a growing set of launch providers now faces questions from regulators and the public about what their rockets do high above the weather.
 Stakeholder Why Artemis II ionosphere data matters Likely response 
 GNSS receiver makers Real-world perturbation examples test correction models Review April 1, 2026 logs and model behavior 
 Satellite operators Electron-content changes alter radio propagation Add launch windows to monitoring plans 
 Launch providers Public attention on environmental effects of heavy-lift flights Prepare plain-language explanations 
 Space agencies Need clear statements to counter overstated headlines Publish primary data and methods 
 Investors in space hardware Headline risk can move sentiment around launch programs Separate measured effects from viral claims 
 The money side is worth watching without exaggerating it. We tracked how space hardware funding jumped 34x to $17B , and a flow of capital that size draws scrutiny. If a false claim about GPS damage gained traction, it could invite regulatory attention to the sector. Accurate reporting protects both the public and the companies involved.
 Competitive Comparison: Launch Effects vs Other Ionospheric Disturbers
 Rocket launches are only one source of ionospheric variation. Solar flares, geomagnetic storms, earthquakes and tropospheric weather also produce measurable TEC changes. For a navigation engineer, the useful question is how a launch compares with the other disturbers in duration, reach and predictability. The verified record gives numbers only for Artemis II, so the comparison below stays qualitative for the other sources.
 Disturbance source Predictable in advance? Typical character Artemis II relevance 
 Heavy-lift rocket launch Yes, scheduled Short-lived waves and localized depletion Launch waves lasted 15 to 20 minutes 
 In-space engine burn Yes, scheduled Exhaust injected at altitude, regional spread ARM spanned about 50 degrees of longitude 
 Geomagnetic storm Partly, by forecast Large-scale, long-lasting changes Not part of the reported Artemis II result 
 Solar flare No Sudden dayside enhancement Not part of the reported result 
 Earthquake or tsunami No Wave signatures after the event Same detection method, different cause 
 The takeaway for planners is that scheduled events are the manageable ones. A launch window is published weeks ahead, and an operator can mark it in a monitoring calendar. A solar flare gives no such warning. That makes the Artemis II disturbances, at 2.5 to 3.7 TECU, a case study in a controllable category of risk. Our November launch calendar lists upcoming dates that fall into the same bucket.
 Why GPS Matters More Beyond Low Earth Orbit
 Artemis II was a lunar mission, and TLI is the burn that sent Orion on its way out. That gives the story an irony. The same navigation constellations that measured the ionosphere cannot fully serve a spacecraft heading for the Moon, so navigation in cislunar space is its own challenge, and agencies are examining how to extend position and timing services outward.
 Our report on how the Space Force weighs five cislunar satellites shows the policy side of that push. Ionospheric behavior matters at the launch and return ends of any lunar trip, because that is where signals cross the plasma. In deep space, the question changes from delay through the ionosphere to geometry and clock accuracy.
 For hardware designers, the lesson is modest and practical. Test receivers against recorded disturbance events. The Artemis II TEC maps, once released in full detail, would make a useful benchmark set because they pair a known cause with a measured response.
 What Artemis III and Later Flights Mean for Monitoring
 The next mission in the program is already taking shape on the ground. We reported that the Artemis III core stage, 212 feet tall, joined its boosters in the VAB . Each future SLS launch gives researchers another chance to compare results with the April 1, 2026 data. If the pattern repeats, the disturbance amplitudes and propagation speeds should land in a similar range. If they do not, that difference becomes a finding in its own right.

 Repeat observations also settle questions a single flight cannot. One launch cannot separate the effect of the rocket from the effect of that day’s ionospheric weather. A second and third launch under different conditions can. Researchers will likely want matched control days, meaning days without launches, to separate the signal from natural variation.
 Program politics add a wrinkle. Funding fights around the lunar plan, which we covered in the $2.89B lander debate , shape how often and how fast flights happen. Fewer flights mean fewer natural experiments. That is an indirect effect, but it is real for the scientists waiting on data.
 Five Predictions for the Artemis II Ionosphere Story
 These are my own forecasts, labeled as such. None comes from a named source, and none is a fact.
 The “GPS disruption” claim will stay unconfirmed. I expect no agency to document a service outage tied to Artemis II, because the record so far points to detection rather than failure.
 Secondary figures will get quietly dropped. The 3,500 station and 5,000 km numbers will either gain a primary source or fade from republished versions within weeks.
 Receiver makers will cite the event. Expect GNSS vendors to use the April 1 data as a worked example in technical notes and conference talks.
 Artemis III will draw a repeat measurement. Ground networks will likely monitor the next SLS launch with the Artemis II numbers as the baseline.
 Launch operators will publish plainer environmental summaries. Public attention to atmospheric effects will push providers to explain their plumes in simple terms before a headline does it for them.
 The riskiest of these is the second. Viral numbers sometimes outlive their weak sources, and a figure that sounds precise gets repeated for months. I would still bet on the correction, since the specific numbers lack backing in the verified material.
 How to Read a Viral Space Headline Without Getting Burned
 The Artemis II episode offers a quick checklist for readers and for editors. First, separate the instrument from the subject. If GPS data revealed an effect, GPS worked. Second, look for the unit. A claim with TECU, meters per second and minutes attached has a measurement behind it. A claim with only adjectives like “huge” does not. Third, ask who said it. A named researcher or agency on the record carries weight, while an unattributed “reports say” does not.
 Fourth, check whether the headline verb matches the data. “Tore a hole” is a strong verb. The research record uses language about disturbances, perturbations and effects. When the verb in the headline is stronger than the verb in the paper, the headline has added something. Fifth, hunt for the secondary-source tell. Numbers that appear in only one non-primary report, like the 3,500 stations, deserve a pause before you share them.
 None of this makes the real result less interesting. A lunar mission that left a mappable signature across roughly 50 degrees of longitude is a good story on its own. It needs no embellishment, and the embellishment is what turns a solid result into a correction request.
 Bottom Line for Hardware Teams and Readers
 The verified story is this: Artemis II, launched April 1, 2026 on SLS from Kennedy Space Center, produced ionospheric disturbances at launch, ARM and TLI. Researchers measured them with GPS and GLONASS TEC data. The ARM and TLI amplitudes ran about 2.5 to 3.7 TECU. The ARM disturbance covered about 50 degrees of longitude across North America. Launch waves moved at 600 to 1,500 m/s and lasted 15 to 20 minutes.
 The unverified story is the one that spread. A “hole” is wording, not a measurement. A GPS disruption has no documented outage behind it. The 3,500 stations and 5,000 km appear in a secondary report and nowhere in the authoritative record we checked. No named NASA official or researcher is on record saying Artemis II knocked out GPS.
 For engineers, the action item is small. Pull your own timing and positioning logs for the launch and burn windows, and see whether anything shows up. If nothing does, you have your answer faster than any news cycle will give it. For everyone else, the takeaway: a satellite network that can see the atmosphere ripple is a network doing its job.
 FAQ: Artemis II, the Ionosphere and GPS
 Did Artemis II really tear a hole in the atmosphere? The verified record does not use that language. Researchers reported ionospheric disturbances linked to the launch, the Apogee Raise Maneuver and Trans-Lunar Injection. The “hole” wording comes from headlines and has no measurement behind it.
 Did the launch disrupt GPS signals? That is not confirmed. The available record supports GPS-based detection of ionospheric variations, and it documents no GPS outage, degradation or operational disruption. No named NASA official or researcher is on record claiming one.
 How big were the disturbances? The reported ARM and TLI amplitudes ran from roughly 2.5 to 3.7 TECU. The ARM disturbance extended about 50 degrees of longitude across North America. Launch-driven acoustic and gravity waves moved at 600 to 1,500 meters per second and lasted 15 to 20 minutes.
 What is a TECU? It is the unit of total electron content, equal to 10^16 electrons per square meter along a signal path. Scientists derive it by comparing signal delays on different frequencies from navigation satellites such as GPS and GLONASS.
 Where do the 3,500 stations and 5,000 km figures come from? They appear in a secondary report. The authoritative material available for this article does not corroborate them, so treat them as unverified until a primary source states them.
 When and where did Artemis II launch? It launched on April 1, 2026 from Kennedy Space Center on NASA’s Space Launch System rocket, carrying the Orion spacecraft.
 How much thrust does the SLS core stage produce? The core stage is listed with 8,896 kN of thrust. That figure covers the core stage alone and does not include the side boosters.
